L145:        waitid()
L146:            The waitid() system call (available since Linux 2.6.9) provides
L147:            more precise control over which child state changes to wait for.
L148: 
L149:            The idtype and id arguments select the child(ren) to wait for, as
L150:            follows:
L151: 
L152:            idtype == P_PID
L153:                   Wait for the child whose process ID matches id.
L154: 
L155:            idtype == P_PIDFD (since Linux 5.4)
L156:                   Wait for the child referred to by the PID file descriptor
L157:                   specified in id.  (See cite24†pidfd_open(2) for further
L158:                   information on PID file descriptors.)
L159: 
L160:            idtype == P_PGID
L161:                   Wait for any child whose process group ID matches id.
L162:                   Since Linux 5.4, if id is zero, then wait for any child
L163:                   that is in the same process group as the caller's process
L164:                   group at the time of the call.
L165: 
L166:            idtype == P_ALL
L167:                   Wait for any child; id is ignored.
L168:            The child state changes to wait for are specified by ORing one or
L169:            more of the following flags in options:
L170: 
L171:            WEXITED
L172:                   Wait for children that have terminated.
L173: 
L174:            WSTOPPED
L175:                   Wait for children that have been stopped by delivery of a
L176:                   signal.
L177: 
L178:            WCONTINUED
L179:                   Wait for (previously stopped) children that have been
L180:                   resumed by delivery of SIGCONT.
L181:            The following flags may additionally be ORed in options:
L182: 
L183:            WNOHANG
L184:                   As for waitpid().
L185: 
L186:            WNOWAIT
L187:                   Leave the child in a waitable state; a later wait call can
L188:                   be used to again retrieve the child status information.
L189: 
L190:            Upon successful return, waitid() fills in the following fields of
L191:            the siginfo_t structure pointed to by infop:
L192: 
L193:            si_pid The process ID of the child.
L194:            si_uid The real user ID of the child.  (This field is not set on
L195:                   most other implementations.)
L196: 
L197:            si_signo
L198:                   Always set to SIGCHLD.
L199: 
L200:            si_status
L201:                   Either the exit status of the child, as given to cite22†_exit(2) L202:                   (or cite21†exit(3) ), or the signal that caused the child to
L203:                   terminate, stop, or continue.  The si_code field can be
L204:                   used to determine how to interpret this field.
L205: 
L206:            si_code
L207:                   Set to one of: CLD_EXITED (child called cite22†_exit(2) );
L208:                   CLD_KILLED (child killed by signal); CLD_DUMPED (child
L209:                   killed by signal, and dumped core); CLD_STOPPED (child
L210:                   stopped by signal); CLD_TRAPPED (traced child has trapped);
L211:                   or CLD_CONTINUED (child continued by SIGCONT).
L212: 
L213:            If WNOHANG was specified in options and there were no children in
L214:            a waitable state, then waitid() returns 0 immediately and the
L215:            state of the siginfo_t structure pointed to by infop depends on
L216:            the implementation.  To (portably) distinguish this case from that
L217:            where a child was in a waitable state, zero out the si_pid field
L218:            before the call and check for a nonzero value in this field after
L219:            the call returns.
L220: 
L221:            POSIX.1-2008 Technical Corrigendum 1 (2013) adds the requirement
L222:            that when WNOHANG is specified in options and there were no
L223:            children in a waitable state, then waitid() should zero out the
L224:            si_pid and si_signo fields of the structure.  On Linux and other
L225:            implementations that adhere to this requirement, it is not
L226:            necessary to zero out the si_pid field before calling waitid().
L227:            However, not all implementations follow the POSIX.1 specification
L228:            on this point.
L229: ## RETURN VALUE         cite17†top L230: 
L231:            wait(): on success, returns the process ID of the terminated
L232:            child; on failure, -1 is returned.
L233: 
L234:            waitpid(): on success, returns the process ID of the child whose
L235:            state has changed; if WNOHANG was specified and one or more
L236:            child(ren) specified by pid exist, but have not yet changed state,
L237:            then 0 is returned.  On failure, -1 is returned.
L238:            waitid(): returns 0 on success or if WNOHANG was specified and no
L239:            child(ren) specified by id has yet changed state; on failure, -1
L240:            is returned.
L241: 
L242:            On failure, each of these calls sets cite25†errno to indicate the error.
L243: ## ERRORS         cite17†top L244: 
L245:            EAGAIN The PID file descriptor specified in id is nonblocking and
L246:                   the process that it refers to has not terminated.
L247: 
L248:            ECHILD (for wait()) The calling process does not have any
L249:                   unwaited-for children.
L250: 
L251:            ECHILD (for waitpid() or waitid()) The process specified by pid
L252:                   (waitpid()) or idtype and id (waitid()) does not exist or
L253:                   is not a child of the calling process.  (This can happen
L254:                   for one's own child if the action for SIGCHLD is set to
L255:                   SIG_IGN.  See also the Linux Notes section about threads.)
L256: 
L257:            EINTR  WNOHANG was not set and an unblocked signal or a SIGCHLD
L258:                   was caught; see cite26†signal(7) .
L259: 
L260:            EINVAL The options argument was invalid.
L261: 
L262:            ESRCH  (for wait() or waitpid()) pid is equal to INT_MIN.
L263: ## VERSIONS         cite17†top L264: 
L265:        C library/kernel differences
L266:            wait() is actually a library function that (in glibc) is
L267:            implemented as a call to cite27†wait4(2) .
L268: 
L269:            On some architectures, there is no waitpid() system call; instead,
L270:            this interface is implemented via a C library wrapper function
L271:            that calls cite27†wait4(2) .
L272: 
L273:            The raw waitid() system call takes a fifth argument, of type
L274:            struct rusage *.  If this argument is non-NULL, then it is used to
L275:            return resource usage information about the child, in the same
L276:            manner as cite27†wait4(2) .  See cite28†getrusage(2) for details.
L277: ## STANDARDS         cite17†top L278: 
L279:            POSIX.1-2024.

L282: ## HISTORY         cite17†top L283: 
L284:            SVr4, 4.3BSD, POSIX.1-2001.
L285: ## NOTES         cite17†top L286: 
L287:            A child that terminates, but has not been waited for becomes a
L288:            "zombie".  The kernel maintains a minimal set of information about
L289:            the zombie process (PID, termination status, resource usage
L290:            information) in order to allow the parent to later perform a wait
L291:            to obtain information about the child.  As long as a zombie is not
L292:            removed from the system via a wait, it will consume a slot in the
L293:            kernel process table, and if this table fills, it will not be
L294:            possible to create further processes.  If a parent process
L295:            terminates, then its "zombie" children (if any) are adopted by
L296:            cite29†init(1) , (or by the nearest "subreaper" process as defined through
L297:            the use of the cite30†prctl(2) PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER operation); cite29†init(1) L298:            automatically performs a wait to remove the zombies.
L299:            POSIX.1-2001 specifies that if the disposition of SIGCHLD is set
L300:            to SIG_IGN or the SA_NOCLDWAIT flag is set for SIGCHLD (see
L301:            cite19†sigaction(2) ), then children that terminate do not become zombies
L302:            and a call to wait() or waitpid() will block until all children
L303:            have terminated, and then fail with cite25†errno set to ECHILD.  (The
L304:            original POSIX standard left the behavior of setting SIGCHLD to
L305:            SIG_IGN unspecified.  Note that even though the default
L306:            disposition of SIGCHLD is "ignore", explicitly setting the
L307:            disposition to SIG_IGN results in different treatment of zombie
L308:            process children.)
L309: 
L310:            Linux 2.6 conforms to the POSIX requirements.  However, Linux 2.4
L311:            (and earlier) does not: if a wait() or waitpid() call is made
L312:            while SIGCHLD is being ignored, the call behaves just as though
L313:            SIGCHLD were not being ignored, that is, the call blocks until the
L314:            next child terminates and then returns the process ID and status
L315:            of that child.
L316: 
L317:        Linux notes
L318:            In the Linux kernel, a kernel-scheduled thread is not a distinct
L319:            construct from a process.  Instead, a thread is simply a process
L320:            that is created using the Linux-unique cite31†clone(2) system call; other
L321:            routines such as the portable cite32†pthread_create(3) call are
L322:            implemented using cite31†clone(2) .  Before Linux 2.4, a thread was just a
L323:            special case of a process, and as a consequence one thread could
L324:            not wait on the children of another thread, even when the latter
L325:            belongs to the same thread group.  However, POSIX prescribes such
L326:            functionality, and since Linux 2.4 a thread can, and by default
L327:            will, wait on children of other threads in the same thread group.
L328:            The following Linux-specific options are for use with children
L329:            created using cite31†clone(2) ; they can also, since Linux 4.7, be used
L330:            with waitid():
L331: 
L332:            __WCLONE
L333:                   Wait for "clone" children only.  If omitted, then wait for
L334:                   "non-clone" children only.  (A "clone" child is one which
L335:                   delivers no signal, or a signal other than SIGCHLD to its
L336:                   parent upon termination.)  This option is ignored if __WALL
L337:                   is also specified.
L338: 
L339:            __WALL (since Linux 2.4)
L340:                   Wait for all children, regardless of type ("clone" or "non-
L341:                   clone").
L342: 
L343:            __WNOTHREAD (since Linux 2.4)
L344:                   Do not wait for children of other threads in the same
L345:                   thread group.  This was the default before Linux 2.4.
L346: 
L347:            Since Linux 4.7, the __WALL flag is automatically implied if the
L348:            child is being ptraced.
L349: ## BUGS         cite17†top L350: 
L351:            According to POSIX.1-2008, an application calling waitid() must
L352:            ensure that infop points to a siginfo_t structure (i.e., that it
L353:            is a non-null pointer).  On Linux, if infop is NULL, waitid()
L354:            succeeds, and returns the process ID of the waited-for child.
L355:            Applications should avoid relying on this inconsistent,
L356:            nonstandard, and unnecessary feature.
L357: ## EXAMPLES         cite17†top L358: 
L359:            The following program demonstrates the use of cite33†fork(2) and
L360:            waitpid().  The program creates a child process.  If no command-
L361:            line argument is supplied to the program, then the child suspends
L362:            its execution using cite34†pause(2) , to allow the user to send signals to
L363:            the child.  Otherwise, if a command-line argument is supplied,
L364:            then the child exits immediately, using the integer supplied on
L365:            the command line as the exit status.  The parent process executes
L366:            a loop that monitors the child using waitpid(), and uses the W*()
L367:            macros described above to analyze the wait status value.
L368: 
L369:            The following shell session demonstrates the use of the program:
L370: 
L371:                $ ./a.out &
L372:                Child PID is 32360
L373:                [1] 32359
L374:                $ kill -STOP 32360
L375:                stopped by signal 19
L376:                $ kill -CONT 32360
L377:                continued
L378:                $ kill -TERM 32360
L379:                killed by signal 15
L380:                [1]+  Done                    ./a.out
L381:                $
L382: 
L383:        Program source
L384: 
L385:            #include <stdint.h>
L386:            #include <stdio.h>
L387:            #include <stdlib.h>
L388:            #include <sys/types.h>
L389:            #include <sys/wait.h>
L390:            #include <unistd.h>
L391: 
L392:            int
L393:            main(int argc, char *argv[])
L394:            {
L395:                int    wstatus;
L396:                pid_t  cpid, w;
L397: 
L398:                cpid = fork();
L399:                if (cpid == -1) {
L400:                    perror("fork");
L401:                    exit(EXIT_FAILURE);
L402:                }
L403: 
L404:                if (cpid == 0) {            /* Code executed by child */
L405:                    printf("Child PID is %jd\n", (intmax_t) getpid());
L406:                    if (argc == 1)
L407:                        pause();                    /* Wait for signals */
L408:                    _exit(atoi(argv[1]));

L12: ## NAME         cite13†top L13: 
L14:            statx - get file status (extended)
L15: ## LIBRARY         cite13†top L16: 
L17:            Standard C library (libc, -lc)
L18: 
L19: 
L20: ## SYNOPSIS         cite13†top L21: 
L22:            #define _GNU_SOURCE          /* See feature_test_macros(7) */
L23:            #include <fcntl.h>           /* Definition of AT_* constants */
L24:            #include <sys/stat.h>
L25: 
L26:            int statx(int dirfd, const char *_Nullable restrict path,
L27:                      int flags, unsigned int mask,
L28:                      struct statx *restrict statxbuf);
L29: ## DESCRIPTION         cite13†top L30: 
L31:            This function returns information about a file, storing it in the
L32:            buffer pointed to by statxbuf.  The returned buffer is a structure
L33:            of the following type:
L34: 
L35:                struct statx {
L36:                    __u32 stx_mask;        /* Mask of bits indicating
L37:                                              filled fields */
L38:                    __u32 stx_blksize;     /* Block size for filesystem I/O */
L39:                    __u64 stx_attributes;  /* Extra file attribute indicators */
L40:                    __u32 stx_nlink;       /* Number of hard links */
L41:                    __u32 stx_uid;         /* User ID of owner */
L42:                    __u32 stx_gid;         /* Group ID of owner */
L43:                    __u16 stx_mode;        /* File type and mode */
L44:                    __u64 stx_ino;         /* Inode number */
L45:                    __u64 stx_size;        /* Total size in bytes */
L46:                    __u64 stx_blocks;      /* Number of 512B blocks allocated */
L47:                    __u64 stx_attributes_mask;
L48:                                           /* Mask to show what's supported
L49:                                              in stx_attributes */
L50: 
L51:                    /* The following fields are file timestamps */
L52:                    struct statx_timestamp stx_atime;  /* Last access */
L53:                    struct statx_timestamp stx_btime;  /* Creation */
L54:                    struct statx_timestamp stx_ctime;  /* Last status change */
L55:                    struct statx_timestamp stx_mtime;  /* Last modification */
L56: 
L57:                    /* If this file represents a device, then the next two
L58:                       fields contain the ID of the device */
L59:                    __u32 stx_rdev_major;  /* Major ID */
L60:                    __u32 stx_rdev_minor;  /* Minor ID */
L61: 
L62:                    /* The next two fields contain the ID of the device
L63:                       containing the filesystem where the file resides */
L64:                    __u32 stx_dev_major;   /* Major ID */
L65:                    __u32 stx_dev_minor;   /* Minor ID */
L66: 
L67:                    __u64 stx_mnt_id;      /* Mount ID */
L68: 
L69:                    /* Direct I/O alignment restrictions */
L70:                    __u32 stx_dio_mem_align;
L71:                    __u32 stx_dio_offset_align;
L72: 
L73:                    __u64 stx_subvol;      /* Subvolume identifier */
L74:                    /* Direct I/O atomic write limits */
L75:                    __u32 stx_atomic_write_unit_min;
L76:                    __u32 stx_atomic_write_unit_max;
L77:                    __u32 stx_atomic_write_segments_max;
L78: 
L79:                    /* File offset alignment for direct I/O reads */
L80:                    __u32 stx_dio_read_offset_align;
L81: 
L82:                    /* Direct I/O atomic write max opt limit */
L83:                    __u32 stx_atomic_write_unit_max_opt;
L84:                };
L85:            The file timestamps are structures of the following type:
L86: 
L87:                struct statx_timestamp {
L88:                    __s64 tv_sec;    /* Seconds since the Epoch (UNIX time) */
L89:                    __u32 tv_nsec;   /* Nanoseconds since tv_sec */
L90:                };
L91: 
L92:            (Note that reserved space and padding is omitted.)
L93: 
L94:        Invoking statx():
L95:            To access a file's status, no permissions are required on the file
L96:            itself, but in the case of statx() with a pathname, execute
L97:            (search) permission is required on all of the directories in path
L98:            that lead to the file.
L99: 
L100:            statx() uses path, dirfd, and flags to identify the target file in
L101:            one of the following ways:
L102: 
L103:            An absolute pathname
L104:                   If path begins with a slash, then it is an absolute
L105:                   pathname that identifies the target file.  In this case,
L106:                   dirfd is ignored.
L107: 
L108:            A relative pathname
L109:                   If path is a string that begins with a character other than
L110:                   a slash and dirfd is AT_FDCWD, then path is a relative
L111:                   pathname that is interpreted relative to the process's
L112:                   current working directory.
L113: 
L114:            A directory-relative pathname
L115:                   If path is a string that begins with a character other than
L116:                   a slash and dirfd is a file descriptor that refers to a
L117:                   directory, then path is a relative pathname that is
L118:                   interpreted relative to the directory referred to by dirfd.
L119:                   (See cite14†openat(2) for an explanation of why this is useful.)
L120: 
L121:            By file descriptor
L122:                   If path is an empty string (or NULL since Linux 6.11) and
L123:                   the AT_EMPTY_PATH flag is specified in flags (see below),
L124:                   then the target file is the one referred to by the file
L125:                   descriptor dirfd.
L126: 
L127:            flags can be used to influence a pathname-based lookup.  A value
L128:            for flags is constructed by ORing together zero or more of the
L129:            following constants:
L130: 
L131:            AT_EMPTY_PATH
L132:                   If path is an empty string (or NULL since Linux 6.11),
L133:                   operate on the file referred to by dirfd (which may have
L134:                   been obtained using the cite15†open(2) O_PATH flag).  In this
L135:                   case, dirfd can refer to any type of file, not just a
L136:                   directory.
L137: 
L138:                   If dirfd is AT_FDCWD, the call operates on the current
L139:                   working directory.
L140: 
L141:            AT_NO_AUTOMOUNT
L142:                   Don't automount the terminal ("basename") component of path
L143:                   if it is a directory that is an automount point.  This
L144:                   allows the caller to gather attributes of an automount
L145:                   point (rather than the location it would mount).  This flag
L146:                   has no effect if the mount point has already been mounted
L147:                   over.
L148: 
L149:                   The AT_NO_AUTOMOUNT flag can be used in tools that scan
L150:                   directories to prevent mass-automounting of a directory of
L151:                   automount points.
L152:                   All of cite16†stat(2) , cite17†lstat(2) , and cite18†fstatat(2) act as though
L153:                   AT_NO_AUTOMOUNT was set.
L154: 
L155:            AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW
L156:                   If path is a symbolic link, do not dereference it: instead
L157:                   return information about the link itself, like cite17†lstat(2) .
L158: 
L159:            flags can also be used to control what sort of synchronization the
L160:            kernel will do when querying a file on a remote filesystem.  This
L161:            is done by ORing in one of the following values:
L162: 
L163:            AT_STATX_SYNC_AS_STAT
L164:                   Do whatever cite16†stat(2) does.  This is the default and is very
L165:                   much filesystem-specific.
L166: 
L167:            AT_STATX_FORCE_SYNC
L168:                   Force the attributes to be synchronized with the server.
L169:                   This may require that a network filesystem perform a data
L170:                   writeback to get the timestamps correct.
L171: 
L172:            AT_STATX_DONT_SYNC
L173:                   Don't synchronize anything, but rather just take whatever
L174:                   the system has cached if possible.  This may mean that the
L175:                   information returned is approximate, but, on a network
L176:                   filesystem, it may not involve a round trip to the server -
L177:                   even if no lease is held.
L178: 
L179:            The mask argument to statx() is used to tell the kernel which
L180:            fields the caller is interested in.  mask is an ORed combination
L181:            of the following constants:
L182: 
L183:             STATX_TYPE             Want stx_mode & S_IFMT
L184:             STATX_MODE             Want stx_mode & ~S_IFMT
L185:             STATX_NLINK            Want stx_nlink
L186:             STATX_UID              Want stx_uid
L187:             STATX_GID              Want stx_gid
L188:             STATX_ATIME            Want stx_atime

L212:            Note that, in general, the kernel does not reject values in mask
L213:            other than the above.  (For an exception, see EINVAL in errors.)
L214:            Instead, it simply informs the caller which values are supported
L215:            by this kernel and filesystem via the statx.stx_mask field.
L216:            Therefore, do not simply set mask to UINT_MAX (all bits set), as
L217:            one or more bits may, in the future, be used to specify an
L218:            extension to the buffer.
L219: 
L220:        The returned information
L221:            The status information for the target file is returned in the
L222:            statx structure pointed to by statxbuf.  Included in this is
L223:            stx_mask which indicates what other information has been returned.
L224:            stx_mask has the same format as the mask argument and bits are set
L225:            in it to indicate which fields have been filled in.
L226: 
L227:            It should be noted that the kernel may return fields that weren't
L228:            requested and may fail to return fields that were requested,
L229:            depending on what the backing filesystem supports.  (Fields that
L230:            are given values despite being unrequested can just be ignored.)
L231:            In either case, stx_mask will not be equal mask.
L232: 
L233:            If a filesystem does not support a field or if it has an
L234:            unrepresentable value (for instance, a file with an exotic type),
L235:            then the mask bit corresponding to that field will be cleared in
L236:            stx_mask even if the user asked for it and a dummy value will be
L237:            filled in for compatibility purposes if one is available (e.g., a
L238:            dummy UID and GID may be specified to mount under some
L239:            circumstances).
L240: 
L241:            A filesystem may also fill in fields that the caller didn't ask
L242:            for if it has values for them available and the information is
L243:            available at no extra cost.  If this happens, the corresponding
L244:            bits will be set in stx_mask.
L245: 
L246:            Note: for performance and simplicity reasons, different fields in
L247:            the statx structure may contain state information from different
L248:            moments during the execution of the system call.  For example, if
L249:            stx_mode or stx_uid is changed by another process by calling
L250:            cite19†chmod(2) or cite20†chown(2) , stat() might return the old stx_mode
L251:            together with the new stx_uid, or the old stx_uid together with
L252:            the new stx_mode.
L253: 
L254:            Apart from stx_mask (which is described above), the fields in the
L255:            statx structure are:
L256: 
L257:            stx_blksize
L258:                   The "preferred" block size for efficient filesystem I/O.
L259:                   (Writing to a file in smaller chunks may cause an
L260:                   inefficient read-modify-rewrite.)
L261: 
L262:            stx_attributes
L263:                   Further status information about the file (see below for
L264:                   more information).
